name: Valid DFS/BFS Traversal Order Identification
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek graph diya hai aur candidate sequences di hain — poocha hai kaunsi sequence(s) VALID DFS (ya BFS) traversal order ho sakti hain.
whatShouldComeToMind: Simulate DFS/BFS explicitly on the graph, respecting the standard rule (visit neighbors in some consistent order, usually numeric/alphabetic unless stated), and compare against each candidate.
For DFS: once you go deep down a branch, you CANNOT jump to an unrelated branch before backtracking — check this constraint against each candidate directly.
generalSolvingApproach: 2. For DFS: try to actually execute DFS from the stated start vertex, and see if the candidate sequence is ACHIEVABLE by some valid choice of neighbor-visit order at each step.
3. For BFS: verify the candidate respects level-by-level order (all vertices at distance k appear before any vertex at distance k+1).
variationsObserved: BFS on a tree specifically, asking for max/min possible position of a vertex at a known distance — combinatorial counting on top of the traversal itself.
commonTraps: Assuming only ONE unique DFS/BFS order exists — multiple valid orders are usually possible depending on neighbor-visiting choices, unless the question fixes that order explicitly.

name: DFS Edge Classification & Structural Properties
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai edges ko TREE/BACK/FORWARD/CROSS classify karo, ya discovery/finish times ke baare me statement TRUE hai ya nahi, ya connected components ki count nikaalni hai from DFS forest — ye is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (23 me se 11 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: For UNDIRECTED graphs: only TREE and BACK edges exist, no forward/cross.
Use the discovery/finish time interval rules to classify any given edge in a directed graph.
Connected components = n - (tree edge count) relationship.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Run DFS explicitly (mentally or on paper), recording discovery time d[v] and finish time f[v] for each vertex.
2. For each non-tree edge (u,v), apply the interval rules: nested opposite direction = back edge, nested same direction = forward edge, disjoint = cross edge.
3. Remember: if the graph is UNDIRECTED, skip forward/cross entirely — those categories are impossible there.
4. For connected-components questions, count the number of DFS/BFS tree roots needed, or apply n-c=tree-edges.
variationsObserved: DFS tree = BFS tree (same tree from both algorithms) — a strong structural constraint implying specific graph properties (usually means the graph itself has a very restricted structure, like being a tree or having uniform edge patterns).
'First new unvisited vertex' style questions about ancestor-descendant relationships in the DFS tree — reason via discovery-time ordering.
commonTraps: Trying to find forward/cross edges in an undirected graph — they don't exist there.
Mixing up back-edge and forward-edge interval conditions (which one is 'nested going up' vs 'nested going down').

name: BFS Shortest-Path Tree Properties
recognitionClueHinglish: BFS tree ke baare me poocha hai ki ye kis cheez ko correctly compute karta hai, ya distance/level relationships ke baare me claim TRUE hai ya nahi — ye BFS-specific property pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: BFS tree gives shortest path (by EDGE COUNT) from source to every vertex, in an UNWEIGHTED graph — this is BFS's headline property, DFS does NOT share it.
Any non-tree edge in a BFS traversal connects vertices whose BFS-levels differ by AT MOST 1 (can't 'skip' levels).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For 'what does the BFS tree compute' questions: default answer is shortest path FROM THE SOURCE (not between every pair — that needs BFS from every vertex, or a different algorithm entirely).
2. For level-difference claims about non-tree edges, verify against the 'at most 1 level difference' property.
3. For algorithms BUILT on BFS (like double-BFS to find tree diameter), trace the described procedure step by step on the given graph.
variationsObserved: Double-BFS technique (BFS from arbitrary vertex to find a farthest vertex, then BFS again from there) — used for finding tree/graph diameter, a specific composed-algorithm application.
commonTraps: Confusing 'BFS gives shortest path from ONE source' with 'BFS gives all-pairs shortest paths' — it's only single-source.

name: DFS/BFS Time Complexity & Recursion Depth Analysis
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai DFS/BFS ki time complexity kya hai (given representation: adjacency list vs matrix), ya DFS ki maximum possible recursion depth kya hogi — ye complexity-analysis pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Adjacency LIST: O(V+E). Adjacency MATRIX: O(V²) regardless of actual edge sparsity.
Maximum DFS recursion depth = length of the longest possible root-to-deepest-vertex path the DFS could take, which depends on the graph's structure and the ORDER in which neighbors are explored.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Check which representation (list or matrix) the question specifies, apply the corresponding complexity directly.

2. For max recursion depth questions: think about the WORST-CASE neighbor-exploration order that would make DFS go as deep as possible before backtracking — often means finding the longest possible simple path DFS could be forced to trace.
commonTraps: Using O(V+E) blindly even when the question specifies an adjacency MATRIX representation.
